title-group.article-title: Atypical Cervical Myelopathy with Medullary Involvement from Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula: The Steroid Trap

body.p: Cervical myelopathy is most commonly associated with degenerative spondylotic changes; however, vascular etiologies such as dural arteriovenous fistulas (dAVFs), though less frequent, represent critical diagnostic considerations.[1] Intracranial or spinal dAVFs may induce venous hypertension by gaining access to the spinal cord’s venous drainage system, elevating pressure within the perimedullary venous plexus or medullary veins.[2] The fistulous blood flow is transmitted through an anastomotic network linking the pontomesencephalic venous system to both anterior and posterior perimedullary veins, ultimately draining into the coronal venous plexus, which becomes markedly engorged and tortuous. Venous outflow stagnation may occur due to reduced radicular venous drainage within the medullary venous system, which can vary anatomically. Furthermore, the lack of venous valves in the intramedullary veins permits retrograde transmission of elevated pressure from the perimedullary veins, impairing spinal cord perfusion and compromising microvascular circulation.[345] This results in venous congestive myelopathy, which can present clinically with progressive paraparesis or quadriparesis, sensory disturbances, sphincter dysfunction, and in some cases, brainstem-related symptoms such as dysarthria or cranial neuropathies—depending on the level and severity of venous congestion.[678] These manifestations often mimic other neurologic disorders, including demyelinating diseases, motor neuron disease, or intramedullary neoplasms, frequently delaying diagnosis.[9] Intracranial dAVFs are pathological arteriovenous shunts located within the dura mater, connecting meningeal arteries directly to dural venous sinuses or leptomeningeal veins, bypassing the capillary bed. The resulting arteriovenous shunting leads to venous hypertension, which impairs cellular metabolic function and contributes to ischemic injury and neurological dysfunction.[91011]

In this report, we present a rare case of cervical myelopathy with medullary involvement as the initial manifestation of a cranial dural arteriovenous fistula, underscoring the need for a high index of suspicion in atypical or rapidly progressing myelopathy cases.

A 40-year-old male presented with progressive paraplegia and respiratory insufficiency. The cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed long-segment hyperintensity involving the medulla as well as the cervical spinal cord, as shown in Figure 1a. The patient was evaluated for long-segment myelitis, and all the workup was negative. The patient’s neurological status deteriorated following administration of corticosteroids, consistent with steroid-induced worsening of venous-congestive myelopathy. However, on careful review of the MRI of the brain, there were some flow voids in the posterior fossa. Therefore, digital subtraction angiography (DSA) was performed, and a cranial dAVF was diagnosed as the cause of progressive cervical myelopathy. The arterial feeders were from the middle meningeal artery and the dural branch of the occipital artery, with the venous pouch located along the sigmoid sinus, as shown in Figures 1b and 1c. The venous drainage from the pouch was into the spinal veins, as shown in Figures 1d–f, resulting in spinal venous congestion, which eventually led to T2 hyperintensity, i.e., vasogenic edema, in the cord. This resulted in paraparesis, and the medullary involvement was responsible for respiratory insufficiency. Following this, the patient was taken for embolization. A microcatheter was advanced into the dural branch of the middle meningeal artery, and Onyx was injected into the arterial feeder, as shown in Figure 1g. We note penetration of the Onyx into the venous pouch and complete obliteration of the fistula, as shown in Figures 1g-i. On follow-up, there was improvement in bilateral lower-limb power to 4/5, with no respiratory insufficiency.

caption.p: (a) Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) T2w sequence shows T2 hyperintensity involving the cervical cord and medulla (red arrow). (b and c) Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) showed dAVF with feeders from the middle meningeal artery (white arrow) and the dural branch of the occipital artery (black arrow), with a venous pouch located along the sigmoid sinus (blue and red arrows). (d and e) Delayed phase showed drainage into intradural anterior and posterior spinal veins (blue and green arrows), leading to congestion. (f) Dyna CT showing drainage into spinal veins in the midline. (g and h) Microcatheter into the dural branch of the middle meningeal artery with Onyx injection (white arrow). (i) Post-embolization DSA showed complete obliteration of the fistula. CT: computed tomography, dAVF: dural arteriovenous fistula.

body.p: dAVFs are classified based on their venous drainage patterns observed on DSA,[8910] most commonly using the Cognard classification system. Type I lesions exhibit anterograde drainage into a dural venous sinus. Type II lesions demonstrate impaired sinus drainage with reflux into adjacent sinuses (IIa), cortical veins (IIb), or both (IIa + b). Type III dAVFs drain directly into cortical veins without venous ectasia, while Type IV demonstrates similar drainage with associated venous ectasia. Type V lesions—relevant to this case—drain into the spinal perimedullary veins.[67] dAVFs account for approximately 10%–15% of intracranial arteriovenous malformations and are typically diagnosed between the fifth and sixth decades of life.[6] They most frequently occur at the transverse–sigmoid sinus, cavernous sinus, superior sagittal sinus, anterior cranial fossa, and tentorium.[67]

The clinical spectrum of dAVFs is diverse, driven by the lesion’s location and its venous outflow pattern. Cognard type V dAVFs are particularly notable for their potential to cause myelopathy, quadriparesis, cranial neuropathies, and brainstem dysfunction due to retrograde venous hypertension involving the craniocervical junction and brainstem.[10] Wrobel et al. reported cases of cranial dAVFs causing myelopathy via venous drainage into posterior spinal veins through the petrosal vein, affirming the pathophysiological role of venous hypertension rather than arterial insufficiency.[9]

Radiologically, cranial and spinal dAVFs can both show longitudinal cord signal changes, expansion, and perimedullary flow voids. Importantly, spinal dAVFs can induce abnormalities remote from the fistulous site via the coronal venous plexus.[36] However, extension of such signal abnormalities into the medulla has not been documented with spinal dAVFs, as noted by Ernst et al.[8] This distinction underlines the need for cranial DSA when spinal angiography fails to identify a lesion in patients with progressive myelopathy.[67] Brunereau et al., in his series of patients with intracranial dAVFs, showed that spinal draining could only be followed to the cervical level, where the veins were drained into the epidural venous system via a medullary-radicular vein.[110]

Clinically, patients typically present with insidiously progressive motor weakness, gait instability, and urinary dysfunction evolving over weeks to months. Symptoms may worsen with increased intrathoracic pressure during Valsalva maneuvers. MRI typically reveals longitudinally extensive T2 hyperintensities spanning more than three vertebral segments, often without any evidence of compressive pathology. In cases where imaging is equivocal, catheter angiography remains the diagnostic gold standard.[6]

Therapeutically, prompt intervention—either via endovascular embolization or microsurgical disconnection—is essential to arrest disease progression and reverse venous hypertension. The selection of treatment modality is guided by the angioarchitecture of the fistula.[1] Transarterial or transvenous embolization can offer durable occlusion with low complication rates in appropriately selected cases. However, complete obliteration of the draining vein is critical; failure to do so may exacerbate cortical venous reflux or activate collateral shunting pathways. Incomplete treatment of the draining vein or merely targeting arterial feeders is often ineffective and may lead to disease progression. Microsurgical disconnection remains a viable alternative, particularly in anatomically unfavorable cases, and focuses on disconnecting the venous outflow of the fistula to achieve cure.[1348]

This case underscores the imperative to consider cranial dAVFs in the differential diagnosis of progressive, unexplained cervical myelopathy—especially when radiological findings extend into the medulla. Early identification through comprehensive neurovascular imaging can dramatically alter clinical outcomes and prevent irreversible deficits. Importantly, corticosteroid administration should be withheld until vascular etiologies such as dAVFs are conclusively excluded, as steroids may transiently mask or worsen symptoms.
